PSE II · Chapter 23

Gauss's Law & Continuous Charge Distributions

Flux, symmetry & the power of enclosed charge

← PSE II Course

23.0 — A More Elegant Approach

In Chapter 22, we developed the tools to calculate electric fields from charge distributions using Coulomb’s Law and the superposition principle. For continuous charge distributions, this required setting up integrals that could become mathematically challenging — especially for three-dimensional distributions.

In 1835, Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), one of the greatest mathematicians in history, wrote down a theorem that would revolutionize how we calculate electric fields — and then did not publish it. It appeared in 1867, thirty-two years after he set it down and twelve years after his death. Gauss had already made profound contributions to mathematics, astronomy, and physics, including the development of non-Euclidean geometry and the method of least squares; this result sat in a drawer among them.

Gauss’s Law provides an alternative approach to finding electric fields that is remarkably powerful when the charge distribution has symmetry. Rather than summing up contributions from every bit of charge, Gauss’s Law relates the total electric flux through a closed surface to the total charge enclosed within that surface.

Chapter 22 closed by promising that the instinct you built there — look for the symmetry before you set up the integral — would be promoted to a law. This is that law.

“Mathematics is the queen of the sciences and number theory is the queen of mathematics.” — Carl Friedrich Gauss

The elegance of Gauss’s Law lies in its ability to reduce complex three-dimensional integrations to simple algebraic calculations — when symmetry is present. This chapter develops this powerful tool and applies it to several important charge distributions.

*Personal note: Gauss’s Law is mathematically equivalent to Coulomb’s Law — they contain the same physics. However, just as we found that energy methods often simplify mechanics problems in Physics I, Gauss’s Law often simplifies electrostatics problems. The key is recognizing when to use each approach.

23.1 — Electric Field from Continuous Charge Distributions: Review and Extension

Before introducing Gauss’s Law, let us briefly review the direct integration approach from Chapter 22 and extend it to new geometries.

The Superposition Integral

For a continuous charge distribution, the electric field at point P is found by integrating over all infinitesimal charge elements:

\[\vec{E} = k_{e}\int\frac{dq}{r^{2}}\hat{r}\]

where \(dq\) is an infinitesimal charge element, \(r\) is the distance from \(dq\) to point P, and \(\hat{r}\) is the unit vector pointing from \(dq\) toward P.

Charge Density Review

The relationship between \(dq\) and geometry depends on how charge is distributed:

Distribution Type Charge Density Infinitesimal Charge Units
Line (1D) \(\lambda\) = charge/length \(dq = \lambda\, d\ell\) C/m
Surface (2D) \(\sigma\) = charge/area \(dq = \sigma\, dA\) C/m²
Volume (3D) \(\rho\) = charge/volume \(dq = \rho\, dV\) C/m³

The Ring on Its Axis

One geometry we will lean on immediately is the uniformly charged ring of radius \(a\) carrying total charge \(Q\), with P on the axis a distance \(x\) from the centre. It is worth deriving rather than quoting, because it is the semicircular arc of §22.5 with one extra dimension and nothing else new.

The move that made the arc easy applies again: every charge element sits the same distance from P.

\[r = \sqrt{a^{2} + x^{2}} \qquad \text{for every element on the ring}\]

The symmetry is stronger here than it was for the arc. For any element there is a diametrically opposite one, and their components perpendicular to the axis are equal and opposite. Summed around the ring, everything off-axis cancels; only the axial component survives, and the axial fraction of each contribution is \(\cos\theta = x/r\).

\[dE_{x} = \frac{k_{e}\, dq}{r^{2}}\cos\theta = \frac{k_{e}\, dq}{r^{2}}\frac{x}{r} = \frac{k_{e}x\, dq}{r^{3}}\]

Because \(r\) is the same for every element, the entire prefactor is constant and comes straight out of the integral. What is left is just the total charge.

\[E_{x} = \frac{k_{e}x}{r^{3}}\int dq = \frac{k_{e}Qx}{r^{3}}\]

\[\boxed{\;E_{x} = \frac{k_{e}Qx}{\left( a^{2} + x^{2} \right)^{3/2}}\;}\]

Interrogate it along the axis. Three things should be true, and all three are.

  • At the centre, \(x = 0\) gives \(E = 0\). Nothing else is possible: every element is matched by one directly across the ring, so the cancellation is total.
  • Far away, \(x \gg a\) makes the denominator \(x^{3}\) and \(E \rightarrow k_{e}Q/x^{2}\) — a point charge, which is what a ring must look like from far enough off.
  • In between, therefore, \(E\) has to rise from zero and fall back, so it peaks somewhere. Setting \(dE_{x}/dx = 0\) gives \(a^{2} - 2x^{2} = 0\), so the field is strongest at \(x = a/\sqrt{2}\).

That is the whole toolkit from §22.5 reused: choose \(dq\), write \(r\), kill a component by symmetry, integrate what is left, check a limit. We derived it here for one purpose — to build something larger out of it.

Example: Electric Field of a Uniformly Charged Disk

A disk of radius \(R\) has uniform surface charge density \(\sigma\). Find the electric field at a point P on the axis, a distance \(x\) from the center.

Strategy: Treat the disk as a collection of concentric rings. Each ring of radius \(r\) and thickness \(dr\) has area \(dA = 2\pi r\, dr\) and charge \(dq = \sigma\left( 2\pi r\, dr \right)\).

Using our ring result with \(a \rightarrow r\) and \(Q \rightarrow dq\):

\[dE_{x} = \frac{k_{e}x\left( 2\pi\sigma r\, dr \right)}{\left( r^{2} + x^{2} \right)^{3/2}}\]

Integrating from \(r = 0\) to \(r = R\):

\[E_{x} = 2\pi k_{e}\sigma x\int_{0}^{R}\frac{r\, dr}{\left( r^{2} + x^{2} \right)^{3/2}}\]

Using the substitution \(u = r^{2} + x^{2}\):

\[E_{x} = 2\pi k_{e}\sigma\left[ 1 - \frac{x}{\sqrt{R^{2} + x^{2}}} \right]\]

This can be written as:

\[\boxed{\;E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\left[ 1 - \frac{x}{\sqrt{R^{2} + x^{2}}} \right]\;}\]

Check the limits.

  • When \(x \ll R\) (near-field): \(E \approx \sigma/\left( 2\varepsilon_{0} \right)\) — uniform field!
  • When \(R \rightarrow \infty\) (infinite plane): \(E = \sigma/\left( 2\varepsilon_{0} \right)\) — independent of distance!

*This last result is remarkable: an infinite plane of charge creates a uniform electric field that does not depend on how far you are from the plane. We will derive this same result much more simply using Gauss’s Law.

23.2 — Electric Flux

To understand Gauss’s Law, we must first define a new quantity: electric flux. The concept of flux was introduced by Faraday as part of his “lines of force” visualization.

Definition of Electric Flux

Consider a flat surface of area \(A\) in a uniform electric field \(\vec{E}\). If the surface is perpendicular to the field, the electric flux through the surface is defined as:

\[\Phi_{E} = EA\]

The flux represents the “amount of electric field” passing through the surface. In Faraday’s picture, flux counts the number of field lines passing through the surface.

Units: The SI unit of electric flux is N·m²/C, or equivalently, V·m.

Flux Through a Tilted Surface

If the surface makes an angle \(\theta\) with the field (specifically, \(\theta\) is the angle between the field and the normal to the surface), then:

\[\Phi_{E} = EA\cos\theta = \vec{E} \cdot \vec{A}\]

where \(\vec{A}\) is the area vector — a vector perpendicular to the surface with magnitude equal to the area.

Key observations:

  • Maximum flux when surface is perpendicular to field (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)): \(\Phi_{E} = EA\)
  • Zero flux when surface is parallel to field (\(\theta = 90^\circ\)): \(\Phi_{E} = 0\)
  • Flux can be positive or negative depending on orientation

General Definition: Non-uniform Fields

For a non-uniform electric field or a curved surface, we must integrate:

\[\Phi_{E} = \int\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A}\]

where \(d\vec{A}\) is an infinitesimal area element with direction normal to the surface.

Flux Through a Closed Surface

For a closed surface (one that completely encloses a volume, like a sphere or cube), we use the notation:

\[\Phi_{E} = \oint\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A}\]

Convention: For a closed surface, the area vector \(d\vec{A}\) always points outward from the enclosed volume.

This means:

  • Field lines leaving the surface contribute positive flux
  • Field lines entering the surface contribute negative flux

Flux and Field Lines

The flux through a surface is proportional to the net number of field lines passing through:

\[\Phi_{E} \propto \left( \text{lines\ out} \right) - \left( \text{lines\ in} \right)\]

For a closed surface with no charge inside: every field line that enters must also exit, so the net flux is zero.

For a closed surface enclosing a positive charge: more field lines leave than enter, so the net flux is positive.

For a closed surface enclosing a negative charge: more field lines enter than leave, so the net flux is negative.

23.3 — Gauss’s Law

We are now ready to state one of the most important laws in electromagnetism.

Statement of Gauss’s Law

Gauss’s Law: The net electric flux through any closed surface is equal to the net charge enclosed divided by \(\varepsilon_{0}\):

\[\oint\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

where:

  • The integral is over a closed surface (called a Gaussian surface)
  • \(q_{\text{enc}}\) is the total charge inside the Gaussian surface
  • \(\varepsilon_{0} = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}\) C²/(N·m²) is the permittivity of free space

Interpretation

Gauss’s Law tells us that:

  1. Charges are sources of electric field lines. Positive charges are sources (lines emerge); negative charges are sinks (lines terminate).

  2. The flux depends only on enclosed charge. Charges outside the Gaussian surface contribute zero net flux — their field lines enter and exit equally.

  3. The total flux is independent of the shape of the Gaussian surface. Whether you draw a sphere, cube, or irregular blob around a charge, the flux is the same: \(q/\varepsilon_{0}\).

Derivation for a Point Charge

Consider a point charge \(q\) at the center of a spherical Gaussian surface of radius \(r\).

By symmetry:

  • \(\vec{E}\) is radial and has constant magnitude \(E\) on the sphere
  • \(\vec{E}\) is parallel to \(d\vec{A}\) everywhere on the sphere

Therefore:

\[\oint\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = E\oint dA = E\left( 4\pi r^{2} \right)\]

From Coulomb’s Law: \(E = k_{e}q/r^{2} = q/\left( 4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2} \right)\)

Substituting:

\[\oint\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}} \cdot 4\pi r^{2} = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

The \(r^{2}\) terms cancel! This shows why Gauss’s Law works: the \(1/r^{2}\) dependence of the electric field exactly compensates for the \(r^{2}\) growth of the spherical surface area.

*That cancellation is not a coincidence, and it is worth a moment. It works because the surface area of a sphere grows as \(r^{2}\) — precisely as fast as an inverse-square field falls off — and the surface of a sphere grows as \(r^{2}\) because we live in three spatial dimensions. In a two-dimensional universe the field of a point charge would fall as \(1/r\), and in four dimensions as \(1/r^{3}\). Gauss’s Law would still hold in either, but the inverse-square law you memorized would not. The exponent in Coulomb’s Law is a statement about the dimensionality of space.

Gauss’s Law and Coulomb’s Law

Gauss’s Law and Coulomb’s Law are equivalent — each can be derived from the other. They represent the same physics in different mathematical forms:

Coulomb’s Law Gauss’s Law
Describes force between charges Describes flux through surfaces
Directly gives \(\vec{E}\) for point charges Gives \(\vec{E}\) for symmetric distributions
Requires integration for distributions Reduces to algebra with symmetry
Always applicable Most useful with symmetry

The equivalence has a boundary worth naming. Coulomb’s Law is a statement about charges at rest; Gauss’s Law survives into the time-dependent theory and becomes one of Maxwell’s four equations. That is the specific reason Gauss’s Law outlives its origin, and why we meet it again at the end of the course.

23.4 — Applying Gauss’s Law: Strategy and Symmetry

Gauss’s Law is always true, but it is only useful for calculating electric fields when the charge distribution has sufficient symmetry.

Requirements for Using Gauss’s Law

To calculate \(E\) from Gauss’s Law, you need a Gaussian surface where:

  1. \(\vec{E}\) is constant in magnitude over the entire surface (or portions of it)
  2. \(\vec{E}\) is either parallel or perpendicular to \(d\vec{A}\) everywhere

If these conditions are met:

\[\oint\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = E\oint dA = EA\quad\text{(when\ }\vec{E} \parallel d\vec{A}\text{\ everywhere)}\]

Three Fundamental Symmetries

There are three types of symmetry that allow us to use Gauss’s Law effectively:

1. Spherical Symmetry

  • Charge distribution depends only on radial distance from a center point
  • Examples: point charge, uniformly charged sphere, concentric shells
  • Gaussian surface: sphere centered at the point of symmetry
  • \(\vec{E}\) is radial with constant magnitude on the Gaussian sphere

2. Cylindrical Symmetry

  • Charge distribution depends only on perpendicular distance from an axis
  • Examples: infinite line charge, infinite charged cylinder
  • Gaussian surface: cylinder coaxial with the charge distribution
  • \(\vec{E}\) is radial (perpendicular to axis) with constant magnitude on the curved surface

3. Planar Symmetry

  • Charge distribution depends only on distance from a plane
  • Examples: infinite plane of charge, parallel-plate capacitor
  • Gaussian surface: box (or cylinder) with faces parallel to the plane
  • \(\vec{E}\) is perpendicular to the plane with constant magnitude on the end faces

Problem-Solving Strategy

  1. Identify the symmetry of the charge distribution
  2. Choose an appropriate Gaussian surface that exploits the symmetry
  3. Evaluate the flux through the Gaussian surface
  4. Determine the enclosed charge \(q_{\text{enc}}\)
  5. Apply Gauss’s Law and solve for \(E\)

23.5 — Applications of Gauss’s Law

Application 1: Uniformly Charged Solid Sphere

An insulating sphere of radius \(R\) has total charge \(Q\) distributed uniformly throughout its volume. Find the electric field at all points.

Volume charge density: \(\rho = Q/\left( \frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3} \right) = 3Q/\left( 4\pi R^{3} \right)\)

Case A: Outside the sphere (\(r > R\))

Gaussian surface: Sphere of radius \(r > R\), centered at the center of the charged sphere

Enclosed charge: \(q_{\text{enc}} = Q\) (all the charge is inside)

By symmetry: \(\vec{E}\) is radial with constant magnitude \(E\) on the Gaussian surface

Gauss’s Law:

\[E\left( 4\pi r^{2} \right) = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

\[\boxed{\;E = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2}} = \frac{k_{e}Q}{r^{2}}\quad\left( r > R \right)\;}\]

This is identical to the field of a point charge! Outside a uniformly charged sphere, the field behaves as if all the charge were concentrated at the center.

Case B: Inside the sphere (\(r < R\))

Gaussian surface: Sphere of radius \(r < R\)

Enclosed charge: Only the charge within radius \(r\) is enclosed:

\[q_{\text{enc}} = \rho \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3} = Q \cdot \frac{r^{3}}{R^{3}}\]

Gauss’s Law:

\[E\left( 4\pi r^{2} \right) = \frac{Qr^{3}}{\varepsilon_{0}R^{3}}\]

\[\boxed{\;E = \frac{Qr}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{3}} = \frac{k_{e}Q}{R^{3}}r\quad\left( r < R \right)\;}\]

Inside the sphere, the field increases linearly with \(r\)!

Summary: Uniformly Charged Sphere

\[E\left( r \right) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} \frac{k_{e}Q}{R^{3}}r & r < R \\ \\ \frac{k_{e}Q}{r^{2}} & r \geq R \\ \end{matrix} \right.\ \]

Key observations:

  • \(E = 0\) at \(r = 0\) (by symmetry)
  • \(E\) increases linearly inside the sphere
  • \(E\) is continuous at \(r = R\)
  • \(E\) decreases as \(1/r^{2}\) outside the sphere

Putting Numbers on It

Symbolic results are easy to nod at. Let us give the graph a vertical scale. Take a sphere of radius \(R = 5.0\ \text{cm}\) carrying \(Q = + 40\ \text{nC}\) spread uniformly through its volume, and evaluate \(E\) at four radii — two inside, two outside.

Location Formula \(E\) (N/C)
\(r = R/2\) \(k_{e}Qr/R^{3}\) \(7.19 \times 10^{4}\)
\(r = R\) (inside) \(k_{e}Qr/R^{3}\) \(1.44 \times 10^{5}\)
\(r = R\) (outside) \(k_{e}Q/r^{2}\) \(1.44 \times 10^{5}\)
\(r = 2R\) \(k_{e}Q/r^{2}\) \(3.60 \times 10^{4}\)

Read the middle two rows together. Two different formulas, derived from two different Gaussian surfaces enclosing two different amounts of charge, hand back the same number at the boundary. That is what “\(E\) is continuous at \(r = R\)” means, and it is the check worth running on any piecewise result you derive: if the two branches disagree at the seam, one of them is wrong.

The outer two rows carry the scaling. Halving the radius from \(R\) to \(R/2\) halves the field — linear. Doubling it from \(R\) to \(2R\) cuts the field to a quarter — inverse square. Same charge, same sphere; the geometry of where you stand changes the law you are subject to.

*Is \(1.44 \times 10^{5}\ \text{N/C}\) a big field? Air breaks down and sparks at roughly \(3 \times 10^{6}\ \text{N/C}\), so this sphere sits about a factor of twenty below the threshold — charged enough to be worth respecting, not enough to arc. Forty nanocoulombs sounds like nothing. It is not nothing.

Contrast: a Thin Spherical Shell

Now move all of that charge onto the surface. A thin shell of radius \(R\) carries total charge \(Q\) spread uniformly over its surface, with nothing inside.

Outside (\(r > R\)): the Gaussian sphere still encloses all of \(Q\), so nothing changes:

\[E = \frac{k_{e}Q}{r^{2}} \quad (r > R)\]

Inside (\(r < R\)): a Gaussian sphere of radius \(r < R\) encloses no charge at all. Gauss’s Law then gives the result immediately:

\[E\left( 4\pi r^{2} \right) = \frac{0}{\varepsilon_{0}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad E = 0 \quad (r < R)\]

Not “small.” Exactly zero, everywhere inside, no matter where you stand.

Compare the two cases. The solid sphere’s field climbs linearly from the centre and joins smoothly onto \(k_{e}Q/r^{2}\) at the surface. The shell’s field is zero right up to the surface and then jumps discontinuously to \(k_{e}Q/R^{2}\). Same total charge, same outside field, completely different interior — and Gauss’s Law delivers both in two lines because only the enclosed charge ever mattered.

*This is the electrostatic twin of Newton’s shell theorem, which you met in PSE-I: a uniform spherical shell of mass exerts no gravitational force on anything inside it, and pulls on anything outside as though all its mass sat at the centre. Newton needed pages of geometry to prove it. Gauss’s Law gives you the electrical version in one step, because the same inverse-square structure underlies both. It is also why the interior of a closed conductor is a safe place to stand — a point we return to in §23.6.

Application 2: Infinite Line of Charge

An infinitely long line carries uniform charge per unit length \(\lambda\). Find the electric field at distance \(r\) from the line.

Gaussian surface: Cylinder of radius \(r\) and length \(L\), coaxial with the line

Symmetry argument: By symmetry, \(\vec{E}\) points radially outward (or inward if \(\lambda < 0\)) and has constant magnitude at fixed \(r\).

Flux calculation:

  • Through curved surface: \(\Phi_{\text{curved}} = E\left( 2\pi rL \right)\)
  • Through end caps: \(\Phi_{\text{ends}} = 0\) (field is parallel to these surfaces)

Enclosed charge: \(q_{\text{enc}} = \lambda L\)

Gauss’s Law:

\[E\left( 2\pi rL \right) = \frac{\lambda L}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

\[\boxed{\;E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r} = \frac{2k_{e}\lambda}{r}\;}\]

The field from an infinite line charge decreases as \(1/r\), not \(1/r^{2}\)!

Application 3: Uniformly Charged Solid Cylinder

A very long solid cylinder of radius \(R\) carries a uniform volume charge density \(\rho\). Find the electric field both outside and inside it.

This application is worth working carefully because it is the first one that asks for two ideas at once: the cylindrical Gaussian surface of Application 2, and the interior reasoning of Application 1. Neither is new. Only the combination is.

Symmetry: the same as the infinite line — \(\vec{E}\) points radially outward and its magnitude depends only on \(r\). Gaussian surface: a coaxial cylinder of radius \(r\) and length \(\ell\). As before, the end caps contribute no flux, and the curved wall gives \(\Phi = E\left( 2\pi r\ell \right)\).

Case A: Outside the cylinder (\(r > R\))

Enclosed charge: the Gaussian surface encloses a length \(\ell\) of the whole cylinder:

\[q_{\text{enc}} = \rho \cdot \pi R^{2}\ell\]

Gauss’s Law:

\[E\left( 2\pi r\ell \right) = \frac{\rho\pi R^{2}\ell}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

\[\boxed{\;E = \frac{\rho R^{2}}{2\varepsilon_{0}r}\quad\left( r > R \right)\;}\]

Case B: Inside the cylinder (\(r < R\))

Enclosed charge: only the charge inside radius \(r\) counts, so the volume is that of the inner cylinder:

\[q_{\text{enc}} = \rho \cdot \pi r^{2}\ell\]

Gauss’s Law:

\[E\left( 2\pi r\ell \right) = \frac{\rho\pi r^{2}\ell}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

\[\boxed{\;E = \frac{\rho r}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\quad\left( r < R \right)\;}\]

Three things to check, and all three hold.

  • \(\ell\) cancelled in both cases. It had to — you invented it. If a dimension you chose yourself survives into the answer, the surface was chosen badly.
  • The field is continuous at \(r = R\). Setting \(r = R\) in either expression gives \(E = \rho R/2\varepsilon_{0}\). The two derivations were independent, so this agreement is a genuine check, not a restatement.
  • From far away it is a line. Write the charge per unit length as \(\lambda = \rho\pi R^{2}\) and the outside field becomes \(E = \lambda/\left( 2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r \right) = 2k_{e}\lambda/r\) — exactly Application 2. Outside any cylindrically symmetric distribution, only the total charge per length matters, which is the same statement one dimension down as “outside a sphere it looks like a point charge.”

Contrast with a thin shell. If the same total charge sat on the cylinder’s surface instead of throughout its volume, the outside field would be unchanged, but inside there would be no enclosed charge at all and \(E = 0\) everywhere for \(r < R\) — so the field would jump discontinuously at \(r = R\) rather than rising to meet it. Where the charge sits changes the interior completely and the exterior not at all.

Application 4: Infinite Plane of Charge

An infinite plane carries uniform surface charge density \(\sigma\). Find the electric field everywhere.

Gaussian surface: A “pillbox” cylinder with faces parallel to the plane, each of area \(A\)

Symmetry argument: By symmetry, \(\vec{E}\) is perpendicular to the plane and has constant magnitude at fixed distance.

Flux calculation:

  • Through each end face: \(\Phi = EA\) (field parallel to area vector)
  • Through curved surface: \(\Phi = 0\) (field perpendicular to area vector)
  • Total flux: \(\Phi_{E} = 2EA\)

Enclosed charge: \(q_{\text{enc}} = \sigma A\)

Gauss’s Law:

\[2EA = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

\[\boxed{\;E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\;}\]

This remarkable result shows that the field from an infinite plane is uniform — it does not depend on distance from the plane! This is consistent with the limiting case of the charged disk when we let \(R \rightarrow \infty\).

Summary Table: Gauss’s Law Results

Charge Distribution Electric Field Dependence on Distance
Point charge (or outside sphere) \(E = k_{e}Q/r^{2}\) \(1/r^{2}\)
Inside uniform sphere \(E = k_{e}Qr/R^{3}\) Linear in \(r\)
Infinite line charge \(E = 2k_{e}\lambda/r\) \(1/r\)
Outside uniform solid cylinder \(E = \rho R^{2}/\left( 2\varepsilon_{0}r \right)\) \(1/r\)
Inside uniform solid cylinder \(E = \rho r/\left( 2\varepsilon_{0} \right)\) Linear in \(r\)
Infinite plane \(E = \sigma/\left( 2\varepsilon_{0} \right)\) Constant

Read the table by how much the charge is spread out, not by name. A point gives \(1/r^{2}\); spreading it along a line gives \(1/r\); spreading it over a plane gives a constant. And in every case with an interior — sphere or cylinder — the field rises linearly from zero at the centre, because \(q_{\text{enc}}\) grows faster than the surface area does.

23.6 — Conductors in Electrostatic Equilibrium

Gauss’s Law provides powerful insights into the behavior of conductors.

Properties of Conductors in Equilibrium

A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium (no charges moving) has the following properties:

1. The electric field inside a conductor is zero.

Proof: If there were a field inside, free charges would move. In equilibrium, they don’t move, so \(\vec{E} = 0\) inside.

2. Any excess charge resides on the surface.

Proof: Draw a Gaussian surface just inside the conductor’s surface. Since \(\vec{E} = 0\) inside, the flux is zero, so \(q_{\text{enc}} = 0\). Any excess charge must be outside this surface — on the conductor’s surface.

3. The electric field just outside a conductor is perpendicular to the surface.

Proof: If there were a component parallel to the surface, charges would move along the surface. In equilibrium, they don’t move, so \(\vec{E}\) must be perpendicular.

4. On an irregularly shaped conductor, charge accumulates at sharp points.

This explains why lightning rods are pointed — the intense field at the tip ionizes air and provides a path for lightning to follow safely to ground.

Electric Field Just Outside a Conductor

Using a small Gaussian pillbox with one face just outside the conductor and one face inside:

  • Inside face: \(\Phi = 0\) (field is zero inside conductor)
  • Outside face: \(\Phi = EA\) (field perpendicular to surface)
  • Curved surface: \(\Phi = 0\) (negligible for small pillbox)

If the surface charge density is \(\sigma\):

\[EA = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

\[E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

Note this is twice the field from an infinite plane of charge with the same \(\sigma\). The factor of 2 arises because charge on a conductor only produces field on one side (outward), not both sides.

Same Sphere, Two Materials

Property 1 is easy to state and easy to under-read, so it is worth putting a conductor directly beside the insulating sphere of §23.5 and looking at what actually differs.

insulating sphere, \(Q\) through the volume conducting sphere, charge \(Q\)
Where the charge sits spread through the volume entirely on the surface
\(E\) inside \((r<R)\) \(k_{e}Qr/R^{3}\) — rises linearly \(0\)
\(E\) outside \((r>R)\) \(k_{e}Q/r^{2}\) \(k_{e}Q/r^{2}\)
At \(r=R\) continuous jumps from \(0\) to \(k_{e}Q/R^{2}\)

From outside, the two are indistinguishable. Not approximately — exactly. Gauss’s Law asks only what is enclosed, and for \(r > R\) both surfaces enclose \(Q\). How that charge is arranged inside is invisible from outside, provided the arrangement is spherically symmetric. The entire difference is interior.

The result just derived gives the same number by a second route: a conducting sphere has \(\sigma = Q/4\pi R^{2}\), so

\[E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}} = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}R^{2}} = \frac{k_{e}Q}{R^{2}}\]

which is exactly what the Gaussian sphere gives just outside the surface. The pillbox and the sphere agree.

The one-sentence version, and the thing to remember: an insulator’s charge stays where you put it; a conductor’s charge moves until nothing is left pushing it. Every property in this section follows from that — the zero interior field, the surface-only charge, the cavity result below, even the factor of two.

*A caution worth carrying into the problems: “insulating” and “conducting” are not decoration in a problem statement. A uniformly charged insulating shell has a field inside its material; a conducting one does not. Read the word before you draw the surface.

Does This Require a Perfect Conductor?

No. Nothing in the argument used conductivity — only equilibrium. If a field existed inside, free charges would feel a force and move; the fact that they have stopped moving is the statement that the interior field has been cancelled. Resistivity determines how quickly the charges finish rearranging, not whether they do, and for any real conductor that settling is effectively instantaneous on the timescale of a static problem.

A field can persist inside a real conductor only when charge is continuously flowing — that is, when the situation is no longer electrostatic. Then Ohm’s law in local form gives \(\vec{E} = \rho\vec{J}\), and the field is what drives the current. We take that up in Chapter 27. An ideal conductor has \(\rho = 0\) and so has no interior field even while carrying current.

There is also a middle case. An insulator whose bound charges shift slightly under an applied field, without ever breaking free, is a dielectric — it weakens a field inside itself rather than cancelling it. That is Chapter 26.

A Charge Inside a Cavity

Hollow out a cavity inside a solid neutral conductor and suspend a charge \(+q\) inside it, touching nothing. The conductor is forced to respond, and Gauss’s Law tells us exactly how.

Draw a Gaussian surface that lies entirely within the metal and completely surrounds the cavity. Every point of that surface is inside a conductor in equilibrium, so \(\vec{E} = 0\) there, and the flux through it is zero. Gauss’s Law then demands:

\[q_{\text{enc}} = \varepsilon_{0}\Phi_{E} = 0\]

But the surface encloses both the cavity charge and the cavity wall. For the total to vanish, the wall must carry an induced charge of exactly \(q_{\text{wall}} = - q\). The conductor began neutral and nothing was added to it, so conservation of charge drives the balance to the outer surface:

\[\boxed{\;q_{\text{wall}} = -q, \qquad q_{\text{outer}} = +q\;}\]

Physical interpretation. The conductor does not screen the charge — it relays it. An outside observer sees \(+q\) and cannot tell whether it sits in a cavity or is smeared over the surface. More strikingly, moving the charge within the cavity changes nothing outside: the wall redistributes to keep the metal field-free, but the outer surface never learns. If that surface is a sphere of radius \(R\), the exterior field is exactly \(E = k_{e}q/r^{2}\) for \(r > R\) — symmetric however lopsided the cavity or off-center the charge.

The plot makes the point sharper than the algebra does. The shell does not attenuate the field and it does not redirect it — it removes the field from inside itself and hands the identical field back on the far side. An observer outside cannot tell the metal is there.

*Notice that shielding runs in only one direction. A conducting shell protects its contents from the outside world, but it does not hide its contents from the outside world — the charge inside announces itself through the outer surface regardless. A Faraday cage is a one-way mirror, and Gauss’s Law is the reason.

Electrostatic Shielding

Because \(\vec{E} = 0\) inside a conductor, a closed conducting shell shields its interior from external electric fields. This is the principle behind:

  • Faraday cages — protects contents from lightning and electromagnetic interference
  • Shielded cables — protects signals from external interference
  • Car bodies — why you’re safe from lightning inside a car (not because of rubber tires!)

23.7 — Gauss’s Law vs. Direct Integration

When should you use Gauss’s Law versus direct integration?

Use Gauss’s Law when:

  • The charge distribution has spherical, cylindrical, or planar symmetry
  • You only need the magnitude of the field (not components)
  • You want to find the field at specific locations exploiting symmetry

Use Direct Integration when:

  • The charge distribution lacks symmetry
  • You need the field at an arbitrary point
  • You want to verify a Gauss’s Law result

Comparison: A Rod of Finite Length

Take a straight rod of length \(L\) carrying uniform \(\lambda\), and ask for the field at a point off to one side. In §23.5 we found the field of an infinite line in three lines of algebra, using a coaxial cylinder. Chop that same line down to a finite length and Gauss’s Law is useless:

  • The field is no longer perpendicular to the cylinder’s wall — near the ends it tilts inward, so \(\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A}\) varies over the surface
  • \(E\) is not constant over any surface we can draw, so it cannot come out of the integral
  • Flux leaks through the end caps, and we have no way to evaluate it

Direct integration is required — which is exactly the calculation you ran in Chapter 22, and in Homework 1.

Notice what changed and what didn’t. The charge density is identical. The geometry is the same straight line. All that vanished is the translational symmetry — the ends broke it — and with it went the entire method. Symmetry is not a convenience here; it is the whole of the tool’s power.

*Gauss’s Law is still true for the finite rod — the flux through any closed surface enclosing it equals \(Q/\varepsilon_{0}\). What fails is not the law but our ability to use it: we cannot factor \(E\) out of the integral, so the equation is correct and useless at the same time. Knowing which of your tools is about to be useless, before you commit an hour to it, is a large part of what separates a physicist from a calculator.

23.8 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Electric flux \(\Phi_{E}\) measures the “amount of field” passing through a surface:

\[\Phi_{E} = \int\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A}\]

  1. Gauss’s Law states that the flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by \(\varepsilon_{0}\):

\[\oint\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\]

  1. Gauss’s Law is most useful when the charge distribution has spherical, cylindrical, or planar symmetry.

  2. Inside a conductor in equilibrium: \(\vec{E} = 0\), excess charge resides on the surface, and the field outside is perpendicular to the surface.

  3. A charge \(+ q\) in a cavity induces \(- q\) on the cavity wall and drives \(+ q\) to the outer surface. The exterior field is unchanged by moving the charge within the cavity — a conductor shields its contents from the outside, but not from being seen by it.

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Electric flux (uniform field, perpendicular) \(\Phi_{E} = EA\)
Electric flux (general) \(\Phi_{E} = \int\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A}\)
Gauss’s Law \(\oint\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \frac{q_{\text{enc}}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
Field outside charged sphere \(E = \frac{k_{e}Q}{r^{2}}\)
Field inside uniformly charged sphere \(E = \frac{k_{e}Qr}{R^{3}}\)
Field from infinite line charge \(E = \frac{2k_{e}\lambda}{r} = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
Field outside uniform solid cylinder \(E = \frac{\rho R^{2}}{2\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
Field inside uniform solid cylinder \(E = \frac{\rho r}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\)
Field from infinite plane \(E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}}\)
Field just outside conductor \(E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)

Connections to Physics I

Mechanics Concept Electrostatics Analog
Gravitational flux Electric flux
Shell theorem (gravity) Gauss’s Law for spheres
Conservation laws Gauss’s Law relates flux to enclosed charge

The middle row is the one to hold onto. You proved the shell theorem in PSE-I with a page of geometry; §23.5 gets the electrostatic version in three lines, and the \(r < R\) linear result has the same gravitational twin. Both follow from the same inverse-square structure.

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 24, we will introduce electric potential — a scalar quantity related to electric potential energy. Just as we found that energy methods often simplified mechanics problems in Physics I, electric potential will provide an alternative (and often simpler) approach to electrostatics problems.

The electric field and electric potential are closely related:

  • If we know \(V\), we can find \(\vec{E}\) by taking derivatives
  • If we know \(\vec{E}\), we can find \(V\) by integration

Together, Gauss’s Law and electric potential give us a powerful toolkit for analyzing electrostatic systems.

*The journey from Coulomb’s Law to Gauss’s Law represents a shift in perspective: from forces between individual charges to the global properties of electric fields. This shift in viewpoint — from local interactions to field concepts — is one of the great achievements of 19th-century physics and laid the groundwork for Maxwell’s electromagnetic theory.
